This is a revised version of `global_hunger_analysis.Rmd` (v1), which stays unchanged.

v1 had two problems that affect its results:

1.  **Aggregate rows counted as countries.** The World Bank files also contain rows for regions, income groups and "World". v1 treated them as if they were countries.
2.  **Years pooled together.** The scatter plots and correlation tests used every year from 2001 to 2020, although their titles say 2018. The same country therefore appeared up to 20 times.

v2 fixes these one step at a time. Steps 1 and 2 are below. The later steps (plots, correlations, v1 vs v2 table) come after choosing between the two options in Step 2.

## Step 0 – Libraries

All packages are loaded once here, and nowhere else:

-   `dplyr` for all data manipulation.
-   `ggplot2` for all plots.

The CSV files are read with base R's `read.csv()`, so no other package is needed.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Step 0 – Load the data

These are the same four World Bank files as v1, plus one new file: the **country metadata file**. It comes from the same World Bank download (inside each zip) and lists every code with its region and income group.

Details of `read_wb()`:

-   `skip = 4` skips the four title lines at the top of each data file. The metadata file has no title lines, so it uses `skip = 0`.
-   `check.names = FALSE` keeps column names such as `2018` and `Country Code` exactly as they are.
-   `fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM"` handles the invisible marker at the start of the files and accented names such as *Côte d'Ivoire*.
-   Every line in these files ends with a comma, which creates an extra column with no name. dplyr refuses to work with a column that has no name, so `read_wb()` drops it straight after reading. This is the only line that uses base R instead of dplyr.

```{r load-data}
read_wb <- function(path, skip = 4) {
  d <- read.csv(path, skip = skip, check.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
  d[names(d) != ""]   # drop the empty column created by the trailing comma
}

hunger <- read_wb("data/API_SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS_DS2_en_csv_v2_2561.csv")
gini   <- read_wb("data/API_SI.POV.GINI_DS2_en_csv_v2_2566.csv")
school <- read_wb("data/API_SE.PRM.ENRR_DS2_en_csv_v2_5690.csv")
gdp    <- read_wb("data/API_NY.GDP.PCAP.CD_DS2_en_csv_v2_2702.csv")
country_meta <- read_wb("data/Metadata_Country_API_NY.GDP.PCAP.CD_DS2_en_csv_v2_2702.csv", skip = 0)

c(rows_per_data_file = nrow(hunger), rows_in_metadata = nrow(country_meta))
```

## Step 1 – Remove World Bank aggregates

Each data file has **266 rows**:

-   **217 economies** (countries and territories)
-   **48 aggregates**: "World", regions such as "Sub-Saharan Africa", income groups such as "High income", and lending groups such as "IDA only"
-   **1 row called "Not classified"** (code `INX`)

v1 kept all 266.

In the metadata file, every economy has a `Region` and every aggregate has an **empty** `Region`, so I keep only codes with a Region. `INX` is not in the metadata at all, so it is dropped too.

The chunk prints the 48 aggregates, so you can check that no real country is removed.

```{r remove-aggregates}
countries <- country_meta %>%
  filter(Region != "") %>%
  select(code = `Country Code`, Region, IncomeGroup)

aggregates <- country_meta %>%
  filter(Region == "") %>%
  pull(TableName)

c(economies_kept = nrow(countries), aggregates_removed = length(aggregates))
sort(aggregates)
```

## Step 2 – How many countries have complete data?

From here on each country should be **one point**. There are two ways to choose that point:

-   **Option A: 2018 only.** Each country's 2018 value of each indicator. This matches the "2018" in v1's titles, but countries without a 2018 GINI value drop out.
-   **Option B: 2015–2019 average.** For each country and indicator, the average of whichever years between 2015 and 2019 have data. More countries are included. The trade-off is that a country's values can come from different years: for example, a GINI value from 2016 next to hunger averaged over 2015–2019.

A country counts as **complete** when it has all four indicators: hunger, GINI, school enrolment and GDP. The code below builds both versions, counts complete countries and shows their income groups. It also shows how many years of GINI data the Option B countries have.

`value_2018()` and `value_avg()` each return two columns, `code` and `value`, for one indicator. `combine()` then joins the four indicators into one table per option.

```{r completeness}
years_b <- as.character(2015:2019)

# Option A: the 2018 value of one indicator, countries only
value_2018 <- function(d) {
  d %>%
    filter(`Country Code` %in% countries$code) %>%
    select(code = `Country Code`, value = `2018`)
}

# Option B: the 2015-2019 average of one indicator, ignoring missing years
value_avg <- function(d) {
  d %>%
    filter(`Country Code` %in% countries$code) %>%
    mutate(value = rowMeans(across(all_of(years_b)), na.rm = TRUE),
           value = if_else(is.nan(value), NA_real_, value)) %>%   # no data in any year gives NaN
    select(code = `Country Code`, value)
}

combine <- function(get_value) {
  get_value(hunger) %>% rename(Hunger = value) %>%
    inner_join(get_value(gini)   %>% rename(GINI = value),         by = "code") %>%
    inner_join(get_value(school) %>% rename(SchoolEnroll = value), by = "code") %>%
    inner_join(get_value(gdp)    %>% rename(GDP = value),          by = "code")
}

data_a <- combine(value_2018)
data_b <- combine(value_avg)

complete_a <- data_a %>% filter(!is.na(Hunger), !is.na(GINI), !is.na(SchoolEnroll), !is.na(GDP))
complete_b <- data_b %>% filter(!is.na(Hunger), !is.na(GINI), !is.na(SchoolEnroll), !is.na(GDP))

# Countries with data for each indicator, and with all four
count_available <- function(d, complete, label) {
  d %>% summarise(option       = label,
                  Hunger       = sum(!is.na(Hunger)),
                  GINI         = sum(!is.na(GINI)),
                  SchoolEnroll = sum(!is.na(SchoolEnroll)),
                  GDP          = sum(!is.na(GDP)),
                  complete     = nrow(complete))
}
bind_rows(count_available(data_a, complete_a, "A: 2018 only"),
          count_available(data_b, complete_b, "B: 2015-2019 average"))

# Income groups of the complete countries, compared with all 217 economies
bind_rows(complete_a %>% mutate(option = "A: 2018 only"),
          complete_b %>% mutate(option = "B: 2015-2019 average"),
          countries  %>% mutate(option = "All economies")) %>%
  left_join(countries %>% select(code, income = IncomeGroup), by = "code") %>%
  count(option, income)

# Option B only: how many of the 5 years have a GINI value?
gini %>%
  filter(`Country Code` %in% complete_b$code) %>%
  mutate(gini_years = rowSums(!is.na(across(all_of(years_b))))) %>%
  count(gini_years)
```

## Decision: Option B (2015–2019 average)

**Why:**

-   Option B keeps **121 countries**, including 13 low-income countries. Option A keeps 88, with only 6 low-income countries.
-   Hunger is concentrated in the poorest countries, so leaving them out would bias the results towards wealthy, data-rich countries.

**The trade-off:** a country's four values can come from different years within 2015–2019. For 37 of the 121 countries, GINI comes from a single year. Inequality changes slowly, so this matters less than losing countries.

## Step 3 – Final dataset and log GDP

The analysis dataset is the 121 complete countries from Option B. Each country is one row, with the 2015–2019 average of each indicator.

**Why log GDP:**

-   GDP per capita is very right-skewed: it runs from a few hundred US dollars to over US\$100,000.
-   A \$1,000 increase means far more in a poor country than in a rich one.
-   On a log scale, the relationship with hunger is much closer to a straight line, which is what Pearson's correlation measures.

So v2 adds `log_gdp = log10(GDP)`. On this scale, 1 unit means "10 times richer". v1 used raw GDP in its correlation.

**A note on the data:** the World Bank reports undernourishment below 2.5% as 2.5. Many wealthier countries therefore sit exactly at 2.5%.

```{r final-data}
hunger_data <- complete_b %>%
  left_join(countries, by = "code") %>%
  left_join(hunger %>% select(code = `Country Code`, country = `Country Name`), by = "code") %>%
  mutate(log_gdp = log10(GDP))

n_countries <- nrow(hunger_data)
subtitle_b  <- paste0(n_countries, " countries, average of 2015–2019 values. World Bank aggregates excluded.")
note_floor  <- "Hunger below 2.5% is reported by the World Bank as 2.5%."

c(countries = n_countries, at_hunger_floor = sum(hunger_data$Hunger == 2.5))
summary(hunger_data %>% select(Hunger, GINI, SchoolEnroll, GDP, log_gdp))
```

## Step 4 – Plots

There is one plot per factor, with each point a country.

Every title now **describes** what is plotted instead of stating a conclusion. Every subtitle states the data actually used: the number of countries, the years and that aggregates are excluded. The red line is a straight-line (linear) fit, as in v1.

### Hunger vs income inequality (GINI)

```{r plot-gini}
ggplot(hunger_data, aes(x = GINI, y = Hunger)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(title = "Hunger vs income inequality (GINI index)",
       subtitle = subtitle_b,
       caption = note_floor,
       x = "GINI index (higher = more unequal)",
       y = "Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Hunger vs primary school enrolment

```{r plot-school}
ggplot(hunger_data, aes(x = SchoolEnroll, y = Hunger)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red", formula = y ~ x) +
  labs(title = "Hunger vs primary school enrolment",
       subtitle = subtitle_b,
       caption = note_floor,
       x = "Primary school enrolment (% gross)",
       y = "Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Hunger vs GDP per capita (log scale)

The x-axis uses a log scale (`scale_x_log10`), so the straight line is fitted to log GDP. That is the same variable the correlation in Step 5 uses.

```{r plot-gdp}
ggplot(hunger_data, aes(x = GDP, y = Hunger)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "red", formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = function(x) paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "d", big.mark = ","))) +
  labs(title = "Hunger vs GDP per capita (log scale)",
       subtitle = subtitle_b,
       caption = note_floor,
       x = "GDP per capita (current US$, log scale)",
       y = "Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Step 5 – Correlations: Pearson and Spearman

For each factor, I compute two correlations with hunger:

-   **Pearson's r** measures how close the relationship is to a straight line. It is sensitive to outliers and skew. GDP uses `log_gdp`.
-   **Spearman's ρ (rho)** uses ranks instead of values. It only asks whether hunger tends to go down (or up) as the factor goes up, whatever the shape of the relationship. It is less affected by outliers and by the 2.5% floor.
    - Ranks are the same for GDP and log GDP, so Spearman gives the same answer either way.

If both agree, the result does not depend on the choice of method.

All tests use the same 121 countries. `exact = FALSE` tells R to use the standard approximation for Spearman's p-value, because tied values (such as the many 2.5% hunger values) make an exact p-value impossible.

`correlate()` runs both tests for one factor and returns one row. `bind_rows()` stacks the three rows into a table.

```{r correlations}
correlate <- function(x, label) {
  pearson  <- cor.test(x, hunger_data$Hunger, method = "pearson")
  spearman <- cor.test(x, hunger_data$Hunger, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
  tibble(factor     = label,
         pearson_r  = round(unname(pearson$estimate), 3),
         pearson_p  = signif(pearson$p.value, 2),
         spearman_rho = round(unname(spearman$estimate), 3),
         spearman_p = signif(spearman$p.value, 2),
         n          = sum(!is.na(x) & !is.na(hunger_data$Hunger)))
}

v2_correlations <- bind_rows(
  correlate(hunger_data$GINI,         "GINI index"),
  correlate(hunger_data$SchoolEnroll, "Primary school enrolment"),
  correlate(hunger_data$log_gdp,      "GDP per capita (log10)")
)
as.data.frame(v2_correlations)   # data.frame prints p-values more readably than a tibble
```

## Step 6 – v1 vs v2

The v1 numbers are copied from the `cor.test()` output in v1 (`global_hunger_analysis.Rmd`, rendered in `report/`). v1 calculated them differently:

-   All years from 2001 to 2020 pooled together, so `n` counts country-years, not countries.
-   World Bank aggregates included.
-   Pearson only, with raw GDP.

R printed two of the v1 p-values only as "\< 2.2e-16", so they are recorded as `2.2e-16` here. They are upper bounds, not exact values.

```{r v1-vs-v2}
v1_correlations <- tibble(
  factor = c("GINI index", "Primary school enrolment", "GDP per capita (log10)"),
  v1_r   = c(0.405, -0.071, -0.431),          # v1 used raw GDP, not log GDP
  v1_p   = c(2.2e-16, 1.165e-05, 2.2e-16),    # "< 2.2e-16" in v1's output for GINI and GDP
  v1_n   = c(1513, 3837, 4342)                # country-years, aggregates included
)

v1_correlations %>%
  left_join(v2_correlations %>%
              select(factor, v2_pearson_r = pearson_r, v2_pearson_p = pearson_p,
                     v2_spearman_rho = spearman_rho, v2_spearman_p = spearman_p, v2_n = n),
            by = "factor") %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

## Step 7 – Extra checks used in the Findings

Two quick checks back up statements in the Findings:

-   **Raw GDP.** Pearson's r using **raw** GDP instead of log GDP, on the same 121 countries. This shows how much of the change from v1 comes from switching to log GDP.
-   **Links between the factors.** How strongly the three factors are correlated **with each other**. If two factors move together, each one's correlation with hunger may partly reflect the other.

```{r extra-checks}
c(pearson_r_raw_gdp = round(cor(hunger_data$GDP, hunger_data$Hunger), 3))

hunger_data %>%
  select(GINI, SchoolEnroll, log_gdp) %>%
  cor() %>%
  round(2)
```

## Findings

All results below use 121 countries (World Bank aggregates removed), with
each variable averaged over 2015–2019, so each country counts once.

**GDP per capita has the strongest relationship with hunger.** Pearson's r
with log10 GDP is −0.67 (p ≈ 5e-17) and Spearman's ρ is −0.83: richer
countries have much less undernourishment. This is clearly stronger than in
v1 (r = −0.43). Most of the difference comes from using log GDP: with raw
GDP, the same 121 countries give r = −0.42 (Step 7).
Spearman is stronger than Pearson because the relationship is monotonic but
not linear. The World Bank reports all hunger rates below 2.5% as exactly
2.5%, so many richer countries sit on that floor and the trend flattens at
the high-income end. Spearman only measures whether hunger falls as GDP
rises, so it is not affected by that bend.

**Inequality (GINI) is moderately associated with higher hunger.** Pearson's
r = 0.47 (p ≈ 4e-8) and Spearman's ρ = 0.51, slightly stronger than v1's
0.40. Countries with more unequal incomes tend to have higher rates of
undernourishment.

**Primary school enrolment shows no relationship.** Pearson's r = 0.13
(p = 0.16) and Spearman's ρ = −0.03; the two even disagree on direction.
In v1 the correlation was similarly close to zero (r = −0.07), but it was
reported as significant (p ≈ 1e-5). That was an artefact: v1 counted 3,837
country-years, including aggregates, so the same country could appear up to
20 times, once for each year from 2001 to 2020. Treating repeated observations of the same country as independent
(pseudo-replication) inflates n and makes even tiny correlations look
significant. One possible reason for the lack of relationship is that
primary enrolment is high in most countries, leaving little variation, but
this analysis does not test that.

**Limitations.**

- These are correlations, not causes. GDP and inequality are moderately
  correlated with each other (r = −0.33, Step 7), so each correlation may
  partly reflect the other. School enrolment is almost unrelated to GDP
  (r = 0.01) and only weakly related to inequality (r = 0.26).
- Values are averaged over 2015–2019 and can come from different years for
  different countries; 37 countries have only one GINI value in that period.
- The 2.5% reporting floor hides differences among low-hunger countries.

**Next steps.**

1. Fit a multiple regression with all three factors together, to see which
   ones still matter once the others are accounted for.
2. Treat the 2.5% floor properly (e.g. as a censored value) instead of as an
   exact number.
